resources.title: Elements of music
resources.summary: The musical elements the exam describes every piece through, each with Pearson's own definition and the words from the specification's vocabulary list to use for it.

blocks.title: Seven elements
rows: "how high or low sounds are", in the melody and the harmony
melody, conjunct, disjunct, leap, sequence, ostinato, riff, pedal, drone, chord, cadence, dissonance
"the relationship of notes within a scale or mode to a principal note"
major, minor, modal, pentatonic, chromatic, atonal, modulation, relative minor
binary, ternary, rondo, strophic, through-composed, sonata form, introduction, phrase
"the nature and quality of musical sounds"
timbre, articulation, legato, staccato, pizzicato, glissando, harmonics
"the number of parts in a piece of music and how they relate to one another"
monophony, homophony, polyphony, heterophony, imitation, accompaniment, continuo
tempo is the speed; metre is the pattern of strong and weak beats, shown by the time signature; rhythm is how long and short sounds are set against the beat
beat, dotted rhythm, syncopation, swung rhythm, shuffle, triplets
accent, and the symbols such as *f* (*forte*, loud) and *p* (*piano*, quiet)
blocks.note: The quotations are from the specification's vocabulary list, which also defines every word in the third column: the tables below give each meaning in short. Structure is the spec's *form*, and sonority covers *timbre*. The list files pizzicato, glissando and harmonics under performance; they are here because each one changes the sound an instrument makes.

blocks.title: Organisation of pitch: what the words mean
rows: a line of single notes, one after another: the tune
moving by step, to the next note up or down
moving by leaps: the opposite of conjunct
a jump to a note more than a step away
a melody or chord pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch
a short pattern repeated throughout a section or a piece
a note, usually in the bass, held or repeated while the chords change
a note or pair of notes held or repeated for a long time, mostly outside classical music
two or more notes sounding together
the chords that end a phrase
a note that does not belong to the chord

blocks.title: Tonality: what the words mean
rows: based on a mode, an older kind of scale
moving by semitones, such as C to C sharp
the minor key that shares a key signature with a major key: D minor with F major

blocks.title: Structure: what the words mean
rows: two sections, A and B, each usually repeated
a main section that keeps coming back between contrasting episodes: A B A C A
the same music for every verse of a song
different music for some or all of the verses
a large form in three parts: exposition, development, recapitulation
an opening passage that prepares for the first main idea
a short passage, often two or four bars, like a phrase in speech

blocks.title: Sonority: what the words mean
rows: the tone colour of an instrument or voice
how far each note is separated from the next
smooth, with hardly any gap between the notes
detached, with a clear gap between the notes
plucking the strings of a string instrument, not bowing them
a slide from one note to another
high, faint notes a string player makes by touching the string lightly

blocks.title: Texture: what the words mean
rows: one melodic line on its own. Adjective: monophonic
a melody with accompanying parts. Adjective: homophonic
two or more independent melodies at once. Adjective: polyphonic
two or more parts playing the same melody at once, with small differences. Adjective: heterophonic
parts enter one after another with the same melodic idea
the musical background to a main part
the Baroque bass line, played by low strings with a chord instrument such as the harpsichord

blocks.title: Tempo, metre and rhythm: what the words mean
rows: the regular pulse of the music
a dotted note paired with a shorter note
a stressed note where a weak one is expected
pairs of equal notes played long then short, as in jazz
long and short notes taking turns inside triplet groups
three equal notes in the time of two

blocks.title: Dynamics: what the words mean
rows: a note made to stand out, shown by the mark > above or below it

blocks.title: Italian words for volume and speed
blocks.note: The vocabulary list leaves these out as words in common use, naming "allegro, crescendo, rall/entando" as examples, so the exam can use them without explaining them.

blocks.body: **Use them to plan an answer.** Asked to describe a passage, go through the elements in turn and give one precise word for each, with where it happens: *the melody is conjunct at first, then leaps up an octave; the texture is homophonic; the tonality is minor.*

applications.title: Talking about any song
applications.body: The same seven headings describe a pop song as well as a concerto: a riff in the bass is organisation of pitch, a sudden drop to one voice is texture, a key change for the last chorus is tonality.

applications.title: Film music
applications.body: Composers change the elements to change a scene's mood: a slower tempo, a move to a minor key, or a drop from the full orchestra to one unaccompanied instrument, a monophonic texture.

resources.title: Set works at a glance
resources.summary: The eight set works on one page: the area of study each belongs to, who wrote it, the recording Pearson names and the kind of score Pearson sets for it, with a link to the topic that teaches it.

sources.name: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Music set works information

blocks.title: Eight set works, four areas of study
rows: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 in D major, 3rd movement
*Bach Six Concertos for the Margrave of Brandenburg*, European Brandenburg Ensemble, Trevor Pinnock
Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor ("Pathétique"), 1st movement
*Beethoven Piano Sonatas: Pathetique, Moonlight and Appassionata*, Alfred Brendel (piano)
*Henry Purcell. Victorious Love*, Carolyn Sampson (soprano), Laurence Cummings (harpsichord), Anne-Marie Lasla (bass viol)
short score: vocals, piano, guitars (TAB and staff), drums
*Wicked, Original Cast Recording 2003*, Kristin Chenoweth and Idina Menzel
Main Title / Rebel Blockade Runner, from *Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope*
*Star Wars OST*, the original soundtrack, London Symphony Orchestra, John Williams

blocks.note: Section A of the exam asks about six of the eight. Listen to the recording Pearson names, with the score, as you revise. A full score gives every instrument a line of its own. A short score or reduction fits the parts onto a few lines. TAB, short for tablature, writes guitar notes as numbers. The score of *Release* is a table of the vocals, instruments, loops and overall structure, with the solos written out on separate pages.

applications.title: Comparing a set work with a new piece
applications.body: Section B asks you to compare a set work with a piece you have not heard, chosen because it is related to a set work. Knowing Bach and Beethoven well is how you describe an unfamiliar piece in a similar style, such as one by Mozart or Haydn.

applications.title: A playlist for revision
applications.body: Eight pieces, from a Baroque concerto to a Brazilian samba, make one revision playlist. Listening while following the score is revision in itself.

resources.title: Note values and rests
resources.summary: Every note and rest from the semibreve to the semiquaver, how many crotchet beats each lasts, and what a dot and a triplet do.
resources.statusNote: The vocabulary list leaves out note names "(crotchet, minim, etc.)" because the exam assumes you know them, so learn them.

blocks.title: Notes and rests
rows: an open oval with no stem
an open oval with a stem
a filled oval with a stem
a filled oval, a stem and one tail
a filled oval, a stem and two tails
blocks.note: Each rest lasts as long as the note of the same name. In 4/4 time a bar holds four crotchet beats: one semibreve, two minims, or eight quavers. Quavers next to each other are joined by one beam in place of their tails, semiquavers by two.

blocks.title: Time signatures
blocks.note: The top number says how many, the bottom number says of what: 4 stands for crotchets (quarter notes) and 8 for quavers (eighth notes). In simple time each beat splits into two. In compound time each beat is a dotted crotchet and splits into three quavers.

blocks.body:
**A dot** adds half the note's value again: a dotted minim is $2 + 1 = 3$ beats, a dotted crotchet $1 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\tfrac{1}{2}$.

**A triplet** squeezes three notes into the time of two: three triplet quavers take one crotchet beat.

**A dotted rhythm** pairs a dotted note with a short one, such as a dotted quaver and a semiquaver, giving a jagged, jumpy feel.

**Count a bar of 4/4.** Count 1, 2, 3, 4 steadily. A crotchet takes one count and a minim two. Crotchet, crotchet, minim fills the bar: $1 + 1 + 2 = 4$. So does two quavers, a crotchet, a dotted crotchet and a quaver: $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 + 1\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 4$. Say the two quavers as "1 and". If a bar does not add up to 4, a note is wrong.

applications.title: Reading a drum part
applications.body: A rock drummer's hi-hat often plays steady quavers, eight to a bar of 4/4, while the bass drum and the snare drum share the four crotchet beats: bass drum on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.

applications.title: Musical dictation
applications.body: The dictation question asks you to fill in missing notes or rhythms on a score. Counting the beats left in the bar tells you which note values can fit. A bar of 4/4 that already holds a minim and a crotchet has $4 - 2 - 1 = 1$ beat left: one crotchet, two quavers, or a dotted quaver and a semiquaver.

resources.title: Instruments of the orchestra
resources.summary: The four families of the orchestra, the instruments in each, how they make their sound and where they sit, and beyond the orchestra: keyboards, band instruments and voice types.

blocks.title: The orchestra
rows: violin, viola, cello, double bass; the harp
bowing or plucking a string; the harp is only plucked
at the front, nearest the conductor
blowing across a hole (flute, piccolo), or making a reed vibrate: one reed on the clarinet, two on the oboe and bassoon. A reed is a thin strip of cane
behind the strings, in the middle
buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece
tuned, playing notes: timpani (kettledrums), xylophone (wooden bars), glockenspiel (metal bars); untuned: snare drum, bass drum, cymbals
blocks.note: The higher an instrument in its family, the smaller it is: of the four bowed strings the violin is the smallest and the highest, the double bass the largest and the lowest. The same holds for the piccolo and the bassoon, and for the trumpet and the tuba.

blocks.title: Beyond the orchestra
rows: electric guitar, bass guitar, drum kit, keyboards
blocks.note: The specification expects you to recognise the sound of all of these; most can be heard in the eight set works.

applications.title: Film scores
applications.body: A film composer picks a family for a feeling: brass for heroism, as in the *Star Wars* main title, strings for tension or romance, woodwind for something light or pastoral.

applications.title: Baroque bands
applications.body: Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 uses a harpsichord, a keyboard, as a soloist alongside flute and violin, with strings accompanying: an orchestra before the modern one existed.
